title: Memory-Mapped Against Isolated I/O, and How Protection Survives
quickIdea: Where the interface registers live decides the instruction set. Memory-mapped I/O puts them in the ordinary address space, so plain load and store reach them. Isolated (port-mapped) I/O gives them a separate space reached only by special instructions such as IN and OUT.
remember: Memory-mapped: one address space for memory and registers; the decoder, not the instruction, decides which is which; ordinary load/store instructions; no new instruction in the ISA.
Isolated: a second address space with its own read/write control lines; needs privileged IN/OUT style instructions.
Protection in memory-mapped I/O comes from the same address translation and protection that guards kernel memory, so all device access is routed through operating-system routines.
Protection in isolated I/O comes from making the I/O instructions privileged, so a user-mode program traps if it tries one.
Memory-mapped I/O spends address space on registers; isolated I/O keeps the whole memory space but costs extra instruction encoding and extra control lines.

example.prompt: A CPU has a 16-bit address bus and 8-bit ports. Compare the cost of giving the interfaces 256 bytes of memory-mapped space against using isolated I/O with an 8-bit port address.
example.work: Memory-mapped: the 64 KB space is 65,536 bytes, of which 256 go to registers, leaving 65,280 bytes of memory. Isolated: all 65,536 bytes stay memory, and the 8-bit port address gives 256 ports on a separate space, reached by IN/OUT.
example.answer: Memory-mapped costs 256 bytes of memory space and no instruction; isolated costs no memory space but needs privileged I/O instructions and separate I/O read/write lines.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2005 Q.20 asks what protects I/O in a memory-mapped machine, and the wrong option 'I/O protection is not possible' is the trap: because there is no I/O instruction, the protection cannot be an instruction-level privilege test, so it is the operating system plus address protection. The question is really about where the check can live.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2005 Q.20: in a CPU with memory-mapped I/O and no explicit I/O instruction, how is I/O protection ensured?
variations.answer: By operating-system routines: the device registers are ordinary addresses, so the address protection of the machine covers them and user code must enter the kernel to touch them.
variations.why: The option 'hardware trap' is attractive but the trap on a protected address is exactly the mechanism the OS protection uses; the answer that names the policy, not the wire, is the one the key accepts.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does memory-mapped I/O let a machine have a smaller instruction set?
variations.answer: Because the load and store instructions already exist. No IN or OUT opcode, no separate I/O address field and no separate I/O read/write control lines are needed; only the address decoder knows that some addresses are registers.
variations.why: It is the standard argument for memory-mapped I/O in RISC designs such as ARM.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A 32-bit machine with memory-mapped I/O maps a device at 0xF0000000. What must the operating system do so that a user program cannot write there directly?
variations.answer: Mark that page as kernel-only in the page table. A user store then faults, the kernel handles the fault as an illegal access, and legitimate device access happens only inside a system call.
variations.why: It is the memory-mapped counterpart of making IN/OUT privileged.

trap.what: Concluding that memory-mapped I/O cannot be protected because there is no I/O instruction to make privileged.
trap.why: Privilege does not have to attach to an opcode. It can attach to an address: the same protection bits that stop a user program writing kernel data stop it writing a device register.
trap.counterexample: Take the same machine twice. With isolated I/O, user code running OUT traps because the instruction is privileged. With memory-mapped I/O, user code storing to 0xF0000000 traps because the page is not mapped for user mode. Both trap; only the thing being checked differs.

check.question: In a memory-mapped machine, which instruction sends a byte to a device, and what makes the access an I/O access rather than a memory access?
check.answer: An ordinary store instruction; the address decoder recognises the device range and routes the cycle to the interface instead of memory.
check.explanation: Nothing in the instruction marks it as I/O - only the address does. That is why protection must be address-based.
